---
title: Adapting the workflow to your own data
---

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Learning Objectives

- Know which steps of the workflow depend on the dataset, and what to check at each one before running it on your own DIA-NN output
:::

The lessons apply each step to one dataset: plasma from 31 patients in three groups, acquired on a SCIEX instrument and processed with DIA-NN using match-between-runs.
Most of the code runs unchanged on another DIA-NN report.
The steps below are the ones that depend on the dataset, in the order they appear in the lessons.

## Importing the data (lesson 02)

- **The report.**
  We read DIA-NN's main report from a `.parquet` file with `arrow::read_parquet()`.
  If your report is a tab-separated text file, read it with `read.delim()` instead.
  Check with `names()` that the columns used in the lessons (`Run`, `Precursor.Id`, `Protein.Group`, `Genes`, `Precursor.Normalised` and the Q-value columns) are present, since column names can differ between DIA-NN versions.
- **The metadata.**
  You need one row per run, with a column of sample names that match the cleaned run names, a column called `runCol`, and one column for each variable in your design.
  Building it as a spreadsheet and reading it with `readxl::read_excel()` works for any size of experiment.
- **Run names.**
  The regular expression in `sub('\\..*', '', Run)` removes everything after the first full stop, which suits the SCIEX file names in this dataset.
  Print `unique(diann_df$Run)` for your own report and write the pattern that turns those names into your sample names.
  Keep the `stopifnot()` check that follows it: it is what tells you that a run has failed to match the metadata, rather than being dropped silently.

## Filtering (lesson 03)

- **Q-values.**
  With match-between-runs, filter on the run-level (`Q.Value`, `PG.Q.Value`) and library-level (`Lib.Q.Value`, `Lib.PG.Q.Value`) Q-values, as in lesson 03.
  Without match-between-runs, use `Global.Q.Value` and `Global.PG.Q.Value` in place of the library-level columns.
  Check how many precursors each filter removes: if DIA-NN already filtered the report at the same threshold, some filters will remove nothing.
- **Contaminants.**
  The `Cont_` prefix comes from the contaminant sequences added to the FASTA file for this search.
  Look at `Protein.Ids` in your own report to find the prefix your contaminant library uses, or whether it has one at all.
- **Sparse precursors.**
  `filterNA(pNA = 0.75)` keeps precursors observed in at least 25% of samples.
  Compare that threshold with your smallest group: a precursor detected only in a group smaller than 25% of your samples is removed at this step.
- **Samples.**
  If the checks in lesson 02 show a failed run, remove it by subsetting the `QFeatures` object by column, as shown at the end of lesson 03.

## Aggregation (lesson 04)

- We aggregate precursors to proteins on `Protein.Group`, the protein group DIA-NN inferred for each precursor.
  This step does not need changing.
- We import `Precursor.Normalised` and do not normalise again at the protein level.
  This assumes that most peptides do not differ in abundance between your samples.
  If that is not true of your experiment, see "When not to use the normalised quantities" in lesson 02.

## Statistical analysis (lesson 06)

- **Replication filter.**
  The filter keeps proteins quantified in at least 3 samples of every group.
  With 3 samples per group, this requires a protein to be quantified in every sample.
  Choose the minimum from your smallest group, and check which proteins it removes, as in the challenge in lesson 06.
- **Design and contrasts.**
  Change the factor levels in `factor(dia_qf$group, levels = ...)` to your groups, with the reference group first, and write one contrast for each comparison you want to make.
  With two groups, skip the F-test (see "Experiments with two groups" in lesson 06).
- **Save the results.**
  Write the results table to a file at the end of the analysis, so that it can be opened outside R.

## Functional enrichment (lesson 08)

- **Organism.**
  `org.Hs.eg.db` is the human annotation package.
  For another organism, install and load the `OrgDb` package for that organism and pass it as `OrgDb` to `enrichGO()` and `bitr()`.
- **Identifiers.**
  Check how many of your tested proteins map to the annotation, as in the challenge in lesson 08, before interpreting the enrichment.
  If many fail to map, run the enrichment on gene symbols with `keyType = "SYMBOL"`.
- **Universe.**
  Use all the proteins you tested as the universe, mapped in the same way as the proteins of interest.

## Recording what you ran

At the end of your analysis script, record the versions of R and of every package that was loaded:

```{r}
#| label: session-info
#| eval: false
sessionInfo()
```

Package updates can change results, for example when an annotation package is updated, so keep this output with your results.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Key Points

- Most of the workflow runs unchanged on another DIA-NN report; the steps that depend on the dataset are the run-name clean-up, the Q-value columns, the contaminant prefix, the missing-value thresholds, the design and contrasts, and the annotation package
- Each missing-value threshold should be set from the size of the smallest group, and the proteins it removes should be checked
- Save the results table and the output of `sessionInfo()` together
:::
